2
Which quantity could have units of N m V–1?
A
acceleration
B
charge
C
current
D
resistance

hints: Notice that $\text{N m}$ is force times distance, so rewrite the given $\text{N m V}^{-1}$ as joule per volt, $\text{J V}^{-1}$.
Recall how potential difference $V$ is defined from energy transfer $W$ and charge $Q$, namely $V = W/Q$.
Rearrange that definition to make charge the subject and check what unit $W/V$ gives.
walkthrough: Start with the given units: $\text{N}$ times $\text{m}$ is work done, so $1 \text{ N m} = 1 \text{ J}$. The units become $\text{J V}^{-1}$.
Recall the definition of potential difference: $V = W/Q$, where $W$ is energy in joules and $Q$ is charge in coulombs.
Rearrange for charge: $Q = W/V$. Therefore the unit of charge is joule per volt.
That is $\text{C} = \text{J V}^{-1} = \text{N m V}^{-1}$, which matches the quantity charge. This is option B.

A.explanation: Acceleration has units of $\text{m s}^{-2}$, which cannot be built from $\text{N m V}^{-1}$.

B.explanation: Since $V = W/Q$, then $Q = W/V$, so charge in coulombs has units of $\text{J V}^{-1} = \text{N m V}^{-1}$.

C.explanation: Current has units of ampere, $\text{A} = \text{C s}^{-1}$, which includes per second and does not match $\text{N m V}^{-1}$.

D.explanation: Resistance has units of ohm, $\Omega = \text{V A}^{-1}$, which is volt per ampere and does not match $\text{N m V}^{-1}$.
